question: A 30-year-old woman with bilateral otosclerosis (worse on the right) has a right-sided pure conductive hearing loss of 45 dB with an intact tympanic membrane and a type As (shallow) tympanogram. She is keen to avoid wearing a hearing aid. Which management is most appropriate?

answers.text: Right stapedectomy (or stapedotomy) to restore ossicular continuity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Stapedectomy (or the more modern stapedotomy) is the definitive surgical treatment for otosclerosis. It replaces the fixed stapes footplate with a prosthesis, restoring sound conduction. It is appropriate for pure conductive loss with an intact tympanic membrane and normal cochlear reserve.

answers.text: Sodium fluoride therapy to halt the disease process and reverse the hearing loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Sodium fluoride may slow progression of otosclerosis but does not reverse established stapes fixation or restore hearing. It is not a substitute for surgical correction in a patient with significant conductive loss.

answers.text: Myringotomy and grommet insertion to relieve middle ear pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Grommets are used for secretory otitis media (glue ear) with middle ear effusion, not for otosclerosis. The hearing loss in otosclerosis is due to stapes fixation, not effusion — grommets would have no benefit.

Incorrect. BAHA is reserved for patients who are not surgical candidates or who have failed stapedectomy. For a young patient with pure conductive loss and intact cochlear function, stapedectomy is the preferred option and offers the best long-term outcome.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the management block. The definitive treatment for otosclerosis is surgical — stapedectomy or stapedotomy. Sodium fluoride has a limited role in slowing progression but cannot reverse established fixation. Grommets are for effusion, not fixation.

Well done. Stapedectomy is the surgery of choice for otosclerosis with pure conductive hearing loss and adequate cochlear reserve. It corrects the stapes fixation directly and can restore near-normal hearing.
